concept: Given an unsorted array of integers, find the length of the longest sequence of consecutive integers. For example, given [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2], the longest consecutive sequence is [1, 2, 3, 4], so the answer is 4.

solutions.label: Brute Force Search
solutions.summary: For each number, repeatedly search the array for the next consecutive number and track the longest chain found.

solutions.label: Sorting Approach
solutions.summary: Sort the array first, then scan linearly to find the longest run of consecutive numbers, skipping duplicates.

solutions.label: HashSet Optimization
solutions.summary: Store all numbers in a HashSet. For each sequence start (a number whose predecessor is absent), count forward to find the sequence length.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's today's problem. You're given an unsorted array of integers, and you need to find the length of the longest sequence of consecutive numbers. For example, if the input is 100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2, the answer is 4, because 1, 2, 3, 4 form the longest consecutive chain.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So I need to find consecutive integers regardless of their position in the array. A few questions: can the array contain negative numbers or duplicates?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, the array can contain negatives and duplicates. Duplicates should not count twice in a sequence. The array length can be up to one hundred thousand elements.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What should I return if the array is empty?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Return zero for an empty array. For a single element, return one.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So given an unsorted integer array, I return an integer representing the length of the longest chain of consecutive numbers, ignoring duplicates. Let me think through some approaches.

sections.title: Brute Force Search
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Array: 100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2"] --> B["Pick 1: search for 2?"]
    B --> C["Found 2: search for 3?"]
    C --> D["Found 3: search for 4?"]
    D --> E["Found 4: search for 5?"]
    E --> F["Not found. Length = 4"]
    A --> G["Pick 100: search for 101?"]
    G --> H["Not found. Length = 1"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style D fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style E fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style F fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest approach is brute force. For each number in the array, I try to build a consecutive sequence by searching the entire array for the next number each time. I track the maximum length found.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For example, starting at 1, I scan the array for 2, then for 3, then for 4, then for 5 which is missing. That gives a length of 4. I repeat this for every starting number.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time complexity of this approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Each number could start a sequence of length n, and each lookup scans the full array. We do this for all n numbers, so worst case is O of n-cubed. Space is O of 1 since we only track the maximum length.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That's quite slow for large inputs. Can you do better?

sections.title: Sorting Approach
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Array: 100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2"] --> B["Sorted: 1, 2, 3, 4, 100, 200"]
    B --> C["1→2: consecutive, count=2"]
    C --> D["2→3: consecutive, count=3"]
    D --> E["3→4: consecutive, count=4"]
    E --> F["4→100: gap! reset count=1"]
    F --> G["100→200: gap! reset count=1"]
    G --> H["Max length = 4"]
    style A fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style E fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style H fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: If I sort the array first, consecutive numbers will be adjacent. Then I just scan left to right, counting consecutive pairs. When I hit a gap, I reset the counter. I skip duplicates during the scan.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Using our example, after sorting we get 1, 2, 3, 4, 100, 200. Scanning through, 1 to 4 gives a run of 4. Then 100 to 200 is a gap, so we reset. The answer is 4.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good. What about the complexity now?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Sorting takes O of n log n, and the scan is O of n. So overall it's O of n log n time with O of 1 extra space if we sort in place. That's a big improvement over the brute force.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Can we do even better, perhaps in linear time?

sections.title: HashSet Optimization
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Array: 100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2"] --> B["HashSet: 1,2,3,4,100,200"]
    B --> C{"Is 0 in set? No"}
    C -->|"1 is a start"| D["1→2→3→4→stop. Length=4"]
    B --> E{"Is 3 in set? Yes"}
    E -->|"4 is not a start"| F["Skip"]
    B --> G{"Is 99 in set? No"}
    G -->|"100 is a start"| H["100→stop. Length=1"]
    style A fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style B fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style D fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style H fill:#fb923c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight is using a HashSet. First, I add all numbers to the set. Then, for each number, I check if its predecessor exists in the set. If not, this number is the start of a new sequence, and I count forward.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For example, I check if 0 is in the set. It's not, so 1 is a sequence start. I count 1, 2, 3, 4, then 5 is missing, giving length 4. For 4, I check if 3 is in the set. It is, so 4 is not a start and I skip it.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Why is this O of n if you're iterating through each sequence?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Each element is visited at most twice: once in the outer loop and once when counting a sequence. The contains check is O of 1 on average for a HashSet. So the total time is O of n. Space is also O of n for the set.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Excellent. That's a classic trade-off between time and space. Let's summarize everything.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great work. We explored three approaches: brute force at O of n-cubed, sorting at O of n log n, and the HashSet approach at O of n with O of n space.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The main takeaway is that a HashSet lets us identify sequence starts efficiently. By only counting forward from true starting points, we avoid redundant work and achieve linear time.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. The trick of checking whether the predecessor exists is a pattern worth remembering for similar problems involving consecutive or sequential relationships.
